subject: chemistry
pattern: The d- and f-Block Elements carries about 5-6 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: 1-mark definitions (transition element, misch metal, lanthanoid contraction), 2-mark reasoning questions (colour, variable oxidation states, stability of Mn2+), 3-mark lanthanoid contraction or lanthanoid-actinoid comparison, and a 5-mark preparation of K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4 with oxidising reactions. Examiners expect balanced equations and correct ionic equations.

questions.q: What are transition elements? Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not regarded as transition elements?
questions.answer: Transition elements are those elements which have incompletely filled d orbitals in their ground state or in any of their common oxidation states. Zn, Cd and Hg have the configuration $(n-1)d^{10}ns^2$; their d orbitals are completely filled in the ground state and in their common oxidation state (+2), so they are not transition elements.

questions.q: Name the transition element of the 3d series that exhibits the highest oxidation state. What is that oxidation state?
questions.answer: Manganese (Mn) shows the highest oxidation state in the 3d series, +7, as in KMnO$_4$ and Mn$_2$O$_7$. Its configuration is $3d^54s^2$ and all seven electrons (five 3d and two 4s) can take part in bonding. Mn shows oxidation states from +2 to +7.

questions.q: What is misch metal? Mention one use.
questions.answer: Misch metal is an alloy of lanthanoid metals (about 95 percent, mainly Ce, La, Nd) with iron (about 5 percent) and traces of S, C, Ca and Al. It is used in Mg-based alloys for making bullets, shells and lighter flints, and also as a deoxidiser in metallurgy.

questions.q: Why do transition metal ions form coloured compounds? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: In transition metal ions the five d orbitals are split into two sets of different energies in the presence of ligands. Ions with partially filled d orbitals absorb light of a particular wavelength from the visible region to excite an electron from a lower to a higher d level (d-d transition), and the complementary colour is transmitted. Example: Ti$^{3+}$ ($3d^1$) absorbs green-yellow light and appears purple. Sc$^{3+}$ and Zn$^{2+}$ have empty or full d orbitals, so they are colourless.

questions.q: Why do transition elements show variable oxidation states? Give an example.
questions.answer: The (n-1)d and ns electrons have very small energy difference, so in transition elements both ns and (n-1)d electrons can participate in bond formation. Successive oxidation states generally differ by one unit, unlike p-block elements which differ by two. Example: manganese shows +2, +3, +4, +5, +6 and +7 oxidation states; vanadium shows +2 to +5.

questions.q: Mn$^{2+}$ compounds are more stable than Fe$^{2+}$ compounds towards oxidation to the +3 state. Give reason.
questions.answer: Mn$^{2+}$ has the configuration $3d^5$, a half-filled d subshell, which is extra stable due to symmetrical distribution and high exchange energy, so it resists further oxidation. Fe$^{2+}$ has $3d^6$ and on oxidation to Fe$^{3+}$ it attains the stable $3d^5$ configuration, so it is easily oxidised. Hence Mn$^{2+}$ is more stable towards oxidation to +3 than Fe$^{2+}$.

questions.q: Why do transition metals and their compounds show catalytic activity?
questions.answer: Transition metals show catalytic activity because of (i) their ability to exhibit variable oxidation states, so they form unstable intermediates and provide a new path of lower activation energy; and (ii) their large surface area with free valencies, which adsorbs reactants and brings them close together on the surface. Examples: V$_2$O$_5$ in contact process, finely divided Fe in Haber's process, Ni in hydrogenation.

questions.q: Why does the oxidising power of the Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ ion depend on the pH of the solution? Write the equilibrium between chromate and dichromate ions.
questions.answer: Chromate and dichromate ions are interconvertible depending on pH. In acidic medium, orange dichromate forms: 2CrO$_4^{2-}$ + 2H$^+$ $\to$ Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ + H$_2$O. In alkaline medium, yellow chromate forms: Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ + 2OH$^-$ $\to$ 2CrO$_4^{2-}$ + H$_2$O. Dichromate is a strong oxidising agent only in acid medium: Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ + 14H$^+$ + 6e$^-$ $\to$ 2Cr$^{3+}$ + 7H$_2$O.

questions.q: What is lanthanoid contraction? Mention its cause and two consequences.
questions.answer: The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of lanthanoids with increasing atomic number from La to Lu is called lanthanoid contraction. Cause: poor shielding of the nuclear charge by the 4f electrons (diffuse shapes of f orbitals); as nuclear charge increases by one at each step, the outer electrons are pulled in. Consequences: (i) the 4d and 5d series elements (Zr-Hf, Nb-Ta) have almost identical radii and similar properties, making their separation difficult; (ii) basic strength of hydroxides decreases from La(OH)$_3$ to Lu(OH)$_3$.
keywords: decrease in ionic radii La to Lu

questions.q: Distinguish between lanthanoids and actinoids (any three points).
questions.answer: Lanthanoids: (i) 4f orbitals are progressively filled; (ii) show mainly +3 oxidation state (some +2, +4); (iii) most are non-radioactive (except promethium) and their compounds are less basic, with less tendency to form complexes. Actinoids: (i) 5f orbitals are progressively filled; (ii) show a wide range of oxidation states (+3 to +7) because the 5f, 6d and 7s energies are close; (iii) all are radioactive and show greater tendency for complex formation, and their compounds are more basic.

questions.q: Why do transition metals form interstitial compounds and alloys? Mention two properties of interstitial compounds.
questions.answer: Transition metals form interstitial compounds because small atoms such as H, C and N get trapped in the voids (interstices) of the metal crystal lattice, for example TiC, Fe$_3$H, Mn$_4$N. Alloys are formed because the atomic radii of transition metals are similar, so one metal atom can replace another in the lattice, e.g. brass and steel. Properties of interstitial compounds: (i) they are very hard and rigid; (ii) they have high melting points, higher than the pure metals; (iii) they retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert.

questions.q: How is potassium permanganate prepared from pyrolusite? Write the equations.
questions.answer: Step 1: Pyrolusite (MnO$_2$) is fused with KOH in presence of air or an oxidising agent like KNO$_3$ to give green potassium manganate: 2MnO$_2$ + 4KOH + O$_2$ $\to$ 2K$_2$MnO$_4$ + 2H$_2$O. Step 2: The manganate is oxidised (electrolytically in alkaline medium or by passing Cl$_2$/O$_3$ or CO$_2$) to purple permanganate. Electrolytic oxidation: MnO$_4^{2-}$ $\to$ MnO$_4^-$ + e$^-$. In acidic medium: 3MnO$_4^{2-}$ + 4H$^+$ $\to$ 2MnO$_4^-$ + MnO$_2$ + 2H$_2$O. The solution is concentrated and crystals of KMnO$_4$ are obtained.

questions.q: Describe the preparation of potassium dichromate from chromite ore. Write the ionic equations for its oxidising action on (i) Fe$^{2+}$ and (ii) iodide ions in acidic medium.
questions.answer: Preparation: Chromite ore (FeCr$_2$O$_4$) is fused with Na$_2$CO$_3$ in excess air: 4FeCr$_2$O$_4$ + 8Na$_2$CO$_3$ + 7O$_2$ $\to$ 8Na$_2$CrO$_4$ + 2Fe$_2$O$_3$ + 8CO$_2$. The sodium chromate (yellow) is extracted with water and acidified with H$_2$SO$_4$ to give sodium dichromate: 2Na$_2$CrO$_4$ + 2H$^+$ $\to$ Na$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ + 2Na$^+$ + H$_2$O. Treating with KCl gives orange crystals of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$: Na$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ + 2KCl $\to$ K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ + 2NaCl. Oxidising action (acidic medium): (i) Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ + 14H$^+$ + 6Fe$^{2+}$ $\to$ 2Cr$^{3+}$ + 6Fe$^{3+}$ + 7H$_2$O. (ii) Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ + 14H$^+$ + 6I$^-$ $\to$ 2Cr$^{3+}$ + 3I$_2$ + 7H$_2$O.

questions.q: Write the ionic equations for the oxidising action of acidified KMnO$_4$ on (i) Fe$^{2+}$, (ii) oxalate ion and (iii) iodide ion. Mention the colour change observed.
questions.answer: In acidic medium permanganate acts as a strong oxidant: MnO$_4^-$ + 8H$^+$ + 5e$^-$ $\to$ Mn$^{2+}$ + 4H$_2$O. (i) With ferrous ion: MnO$_4^-$ + 8H$^+$ + 5Fe$^{2+}$ $\to$ Mn$^{2+}$ + 4H$_2$O + 5Fe$^{3+}$. (ii) With oxalate: 2MnO$_4^-$ + 16H$^+$ + 5C$_2$O$_4^{2-}$ $\to$ 2Mn$^{2+}$ + 8H$_2$O + 10CO$_2$. (iii) With iodide: 2MnO$_4^-$ + 16H$^+$ + 10I$^-$ $\to$ 2Mn$^{2+}$ + 8H$_2$O + 5I$_2$. In each case the purple colour of MnO$_4^-$ disappears (becomes colourless/pale pink Mn$^{2+}$), so KMnO$_4$ acts as a self indicator in titrations.
